title: Standardize function-calling JSON schema, validation semantics, and structured error model
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: multiple clients and models currently rely on informal or ad-hoc 'function_call' parameter formats. This leads to inconsistent parameter validation, unclear error messages for developers, and compatibility issues when we evolve the contract.

Goal: introduce a canonical JSON-schema-like definition for tool/function parameters returned by models or declared by tools, implement deterministic server-side parameter validation with clear machine-friendly and human-friendly error payloads, and provide a compatibility layer to map legacy contracts to the new schema. The work includes runtime validation, SDK helpers, and a migration path with fallbacks and telemetry.
acceptance_criteria: Define a single, compact schema subset we support (a constrained JSON Schema subset) and publish the normative format in the API spec.
Server performs synchronous validation of model-invoked parameters and returns documented structured errors for any violations (HTTP 400/422 semantics).
SDKs surface validation errors as typed exceptions with machine fields: error_code, parameter_path, expected, received_sample, suggestion.
Compatibility layer accepts legacy 'args' arrays and old typed-only shapes for at least two prior client versions and normalizes them to the new schema at runtime.
Add automated unit + integration tests that cover required/optional fields, type coercion rules, enum validation, pattern/format checks, and nested objects up to depth 3.
Telemetry: validation_error metrics emitted with error_code, route, model_variant, and customer_id (when available) for 90d retention in console-ops.
Documentation: spec page, example schemas, and migration guide published to docs.redwood.ai before release.
No user-visible regressions for existing customers using function-calling before rollout (covered by canary rollout plan).
implementation_notes: Adopt a constrained subset of JSON Schema Draft 2020-12: we will support 'type', 'properties', 'required', 'additionalProperties' (boolean), 'enum', 'pattern', 'format' (email, uri, date-time, uuid), 'minLength'/'maxLength', 'minimum'/'maximum', and 'items' for homogeneous arrays.

Reject/ignore advanced constructs: 'anyOf', 'oneOf', 'allOf', 'if/then/else', refs ($ref) - these complicate runtime validation and cross-language SDK generation. If a model returns these, fail validation with a clear error_code 'unsupported_schema_feature'.

Validation semantics: strict by default. If schema sets 'coerce': true (optional vendor extension), allow integer/float string coercion; otherwise fail with type_mismatch. Document that 'coerce' is an opt-in server-side feature for backwards compatibility.

Error payload shape (top-level JSON response for validation failure): {"error_code": "string", "message": "string", "parameter_path": "dot.notation.or[0]", "expected": "string", "received": "string_sample", "hint": "string" } - we'll serialize as application/json.
Map HTTP codes: 400 for client-specified invalid tool schemas or bad request shapes, 422 for model/tool runtime validation failures (parameters returned by model do not satisfy declared schema).

Compatibility rules: implement a 'schema transformer' layer that can convert older signatures: e.g., legacy positional 'args' -> named properties via a declared 'args_map' on the tool definition. This transformer must be pluggable and have unit tests.

SDK changes: generate typed parameter classes from the supported schema subset. Each SDK will expose a validate(params, schema) helper that returns structured error objects identical to server payloads to keep client and server behavior consistent.

Runtime performance: validation must be vectorized and low-latency. Use a compiled validation path (Rust/Go lib) with precompiled schema bytecode cached per-route to avoid parse+compile on each request. Target 95th percentile validation overhead < 3ms for 1kB payloads on standard infra.
design_decisions: Chose a restricted JSON Schema subset to balance expressivity with runtime cost and SDK generation simplicity.
Prefer explicit, machine-readable error codes to enable programmatic remediations in SDKs and Console automation rules.
Expose 'coerce' as an opt-in vendor extension rather than silently coercing types; decision driven by developer experience vs silent correctness bugs.
Use dot/bracket parameter_path strings (e.g., 'options[0].headers.Content-Type') so frontends can easily highlight fields in UIs.
Return both machine fields and a short human message to reduce back-and-forth between users and support when debugging mis-typed parameters.
test_plan: Unit tests for validator engine covering: type mismatch, missing required, enum mismatch, pattern violation, format failure, boundary values (min/max), nested objects up to depth 3, arrays, and additionalProperties behavior.

Integration tests: simulated model returning parameters for a set of 'functional' tools; exercise full request path (model -> platform validator -> tool execution) and assert correct status codes and error payloads.
Backward compatibility tests: run historical function-calling fixtures produced by previous SDKs (v1.8, v1.9) through transformer to verify normalization.
Performance regression tests on canary infra: validate at target throughput and measure 50/95/99th latency of full request flow with validation enabled.
End-to-end QA script and checklist for Solutions/SE team to exercise with real customer prompts before enabling strict validation on Dedicated clusters.
rollout_plan: Feature-gate behind 'strict_function_schema_validation' flag on the control plane.
Phase 1 (internal): enable for internal org only, monitor errors and fix schema edge-cases (2 days).
Phase 2 (canary): enable for 5% of production traffic with auto-rollback on error-rate regression (1 week).
Phase 3 (opt-in): allow customers to opt into strict validation per-project via Console toggle and provide 'coerce' and 'lenient' modes for migration (2 weeks).

Phase 4 (default): flip on by default for new projects and provide 30-day deprecation warnings for projects still using legacy behavior; fully remove legacy mapping after 6 months with migration tooling.
risk_and_mitigation: Risk: strict validation may break existing customers that relied on loose coercion. Mitigation: provide lenient/coerce modes and console toggle, run a migration runner that scans historical function-call logs and suggests schema updates.
Risk: runtime overhead. Mitigation: precompile schemas, benchmark optimized validator, and add a lightweight cache for common schemas.
Risk: SDK parity across languages. Mitigation: centralize schema-to-code generator and create nightly builds for each SDK with integration smoke tests.
